**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Computer Science 2 (0595), ORDINARY LEVEL, June 2019. Duration: two hours.**

Answer any FIVE questions. All questions carry 20 marks each. For your guidance, the approximate mark for each part of a question is indicated in brackets. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. In calculations, you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. Calculators or Phones are NOT allowed.

questions.enonce_markdown:
A Folder in a computer contains files with total size of 7 GB. In order to backup the files, a number of CDs of size 700 MB are provided.

(i) What do you understand by file backup? (1 mark)

(ii) Give two reasons for file backup. (2 marks)

(iii) Convert 7GB to MB (3 marks)

(iv) How many CDs are required to backup all the files in the folder? (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) File backup (1 mark).** File backup is making a copy of files and keeping it on another storage medium or in another place, so that the data can be restored if the original files are lost or damaged.

**(ii) Two reasons (2 marks, 1 mark each).** Any two of: to recover data after a hardware failure (for example a damaged hard disk); to recover files deleted by mistake; to recover data after a virus attack, theft, fire or flood; to keep an earlier version of a file.

**(iii) Convert 7 GB to MB (3 marks).**

1 GB = 1024 MB, so

$$7 \text{ GB} = 7 \times 1024 \text{ MB} = 7168 \text{ MB}$$

(If 1 GB is taken as 1000 MB, then 7 GB = 7000 MB.)

**(iv) Number of CDs (3 marks).** Divide the total size by the capacity of one CD:

$$\frac{7168}{700} = 10.24$$

10 CDs hold only $10 \times 700 = 7000$ MB, which is less than 7168 MB, so one more CD is needed and the number is rounded **up**: **11 CDs** (the 11th CD holds the last 168 MB).

(With 1 GB = 1000 MB: $7000 \div 700 = 10$ CDs exactly.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Write in full the abbreviation DBMS (1 mark)

(ii) Briefly explain the following as used in DBMS:

- Redundancy (2 marks)
- Consistency (2 marks)
- Normalization (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) DBMS (1 mark).** DBMS stands for **Database Management System**.

**(ii) Terms used in a DBMS**

- **Redundancy (2 marks):** the unnecessary repetition of the same data in several places (several files or tables). It wastes storage space and can lead to inconsistent data.
- **Consistency (2 marks):** the same data has the same value everywhere in the database and follows the rules defined for it, so there are no contradictions. Uncontrolled redundancy is a main cause of inconsistency (for example a customer's address changed in one table but not in another).
- **Normalization (2 marks):** the process of organising the tables and fields of a database, by splitting large tables into smaller related tables, in order to remove redundancy and avoid errors when data is inserted, updated or deleted.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Differentiate between data verification and data validation (2 marks)

(ii) Briefly explain why both data verification and data validation are necessary to ensure the credibility of data in a database (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Verification and validation (2 marks).**

- **Data verification** checks that the data entered into the computer is the same as the original source (it has been copied correctly), for example by typing the data twice (double entry) or by proofreading the entry against the source document.
- **Data validation** is an automatic check made by the computer that the data entered is reasonable and acceptable, for example a range check (age between 0 and 120), a type check (numbers only), a length check or a presence check.

Difference: verification checks accuracy of copying; validation checks that the data is sensible and follows the rules.

**(ii) Why both are necessary (2 marks).** Validation cannot detect a wrong value that is still acceptable (an age of 17 typed as 71 passes a range check), and verification cannot detect data that was already wrong or impossible at the source. Used together, they make sure that the data in the database is accurate, complete and sensible, so users can trust (and take decisions on) the data, which is what credibility means.
